Why Tech Matters

Every phone, solar farm and electric bus starts as an idea about how matter and energy behave. Three things keep that idea moving.

Science

Understand it

Electrons, light and forces follow rules. Learning them is the first step to using them.

Innovation

Build it

Transistors, batteries and motors turned discoveries into tools that fit in a pocket.

Sustainability

Keep it going

Tomorrow's tech has to run on clean energy and be recycled, not dumped.

Road to Tomorrow


1831
Michael Faraday shows that a moving magnet makes current. Generators and motors follow.
1947
Bell Labs builds the first transistor, the switch inside every chip.
1971
Intel's 4004 puts a whole processor on one chip, with about 2,300 transistors.
1991
Sony sells the first commercial lithium ion battery.
2022
The National Ignition Facility gets more fusion energy out than laser energy in.
Tomorrow
Solid state batteries, fusion pilot plants and brain inspired chips are being developed now.

How and Why


Why does my phone get warm?

Each time a transistor switches, a little energy becomes heat, and wires resist current. Billions of switches every second add up, so chips spread heat and sometimes slow themselves down.

How does wireless charging work?

A coil in the pad makes a changing magnetic field. A coil in the phone catches it, and induction turns it back into current.

Why are chips made of silicon?

It is plentiful, forms a stable oxide, and its conductivity can be tuned by adding tiny amounts of other atoms.

How does a touchscreen find my finger?

A grid of tiny capacitors senses the electric field. Your finger changes it at one spot and the controller works out where.

Why do LEDs need resistors?

A lit LED barely resists current, so without help it climbs until the LED burns out. The resistor sets a safe current. Try the Ohm lab.

How can I make a battery last longer?

Avoid heat, avoid sitting at 100% or 0%, and go easy on fast charging. All of these slow chemical wear.
